title: Defending an Opinion: Building a Strong Argument
canDo: Can explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options.
goal: State a clear opinion, give two reasons, and defend it against a challenge.

warmup.prompt: Post this statement on screen: Working from home is better than working in an office. Ask: Do you agree? Defend your answer in one sentence.
warmup.tutorAction: Challenge the student gently with one counter-point, such as But what about teamwork? Let the student respond instantly.

theory.structure: Claim + reason + example + concession (I believe X, because Y. For example, Z. Admittedly, W.)
examples: I believe remote work is effective, because it saves commuting time.
Admittedly, some teams lose focus at home, so good communication matters.
Nevertheless, the overall benefits outweigh the drawbacks.
theory.method: Show the argument frame on screen. Ask guiding questions: Which part is the claim? Where is the concession? Let the student rebuild their warm-up answer using the frame, adding a concession.
theory.checkQuestion: Which connector introduces the concession: admittedly, because, or for example?

comprehension.source: Play a 45-second clip from a business podcast with a fast native speaker, or read this text twice at native speed: The shift to remote work sounds like a win for everyone, but managers are quietly worried. Productivity is harder to measure, and junior staff often miss the informal learning that happens in an office.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What is the main concern of managers? (productivity is harder to measure). Which group misses informal learning? (junior staff).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the speaker sound convinced that remote work is a win, or doubtful? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the tone, such as sounds like a win.

conversation.task: Structured debate: the student takes the side they chose in the warm-up and defends it against the tutor, who argues the opposite. Each turn, the student must give a claim, a reason, and an example. Finish with a two-minute summary of the best argument on either side.
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner and language coach. Share one better word or phrase live in the chat as the student speaks, and do not stop their flow.

mistakes: I think that remote work is good because it is more comfortable.
The bad thing is the team don't talk.

title: Hypothetical Advice: Second Conditional
canDo: Can talk about unreal or unlikely situations and give considered advice on problems in detail.
goal: Discuss hypothetical situations and give advice using if I were you, I would.

warmup.prompt: Post this scenario: A friend is offered a job abroad but does not speak the language. Ask: What would you do in their position?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student answer instantly. Challenge them with one follow-up: Why would you choose that over the other option?

theory.structure: If + past simple, would + base verb (unreal present or future situation)
examples: If I spoke fluent French, I would apply for the job.
If I were you, I would take the course.
If she had more time, she would learn the piano.
theory.method: Show the pattern and two contrasting sentences: a real situation (If it rains, I will stay) and an unreal one (If it rained, I would stay). Ask the student to explain the difference and then give advice to a friend in the warm-up scenario.
theory.checkQuestion: Does the second conditional describe a real possibility or an unlikely one?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at native speed: If the government raised taxes on sugar, many people would probably change their diet. Critics argue that it would hurt low-income families the most, though supporters say the health benefits would be worth it.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What would many people probably change? (their diet). Who do critics think would be hurt most? (low-income families).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the writer present both sides fairly? Ask the student to point to the word that shows the balance, such as though.

conversation.task: Advice clinic: the student advises the tutor on a difficult dilemma (a job offer, a moving decision, a conflict with a colleague). The student must use at least three second conditionals and explain the reasoning for each piece of advice.
phrases: If I were in your position, I would ...
If I had ..., I would have ...
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner and language coach. Challenge the student to defend their advice, and share one stronger phrase live in the chat while they speak.

mistakes: If I was you, I will take the course.
If I have more time, I would learn piano.

title: Regrets and Lessons: Third Conditional
canDo: Can discuss past regrets and missed opportunities, and reflect on the consequences in detail.
goal: Reflect on past decisions and their results using the third conditional.

warmup.prompt: Post this question: What is one decision you would change if you could go back? Ask: What would you do differently?
warmup.tutorAction: Challenge the student to explain the result of the change, not just the change itself.

theory.structure: If + past perfect, would have + past participle (a past decision and its imagined result)
examples: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
She would have been happier if she had taken the job.
If they had left earlier, they would not have missed the train.
theory.method: Show a past situation with its imagined result. Ask guiding questions: Did this happen? Can we change it now? Let the student write one regret and its result aloud.
theory.checkQuestion: Can we change a past result using the third conditional, or does it only describe what might have happened?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at native speed: Many entrepreneurs say they would have started their companies earlier if they had trusted their own judgement. Looking back, one founder admitted that if she had asked for advice sooner, she would have avoided two costly mistakes.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What would entrepreneurs have done earlier? (started their companies). What would the founder have avoided? (two costly mistakes).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the founder bitter or reflective about the past? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the tone, such as looking back.

conversation.task: Life reflection: the student describes two past decisions and their results to the tutor using the third conditional. The tutor asks one probing question each time: What did you learn from that?
phrases: If I had ..., I would have ...
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner. Challenge the student to explain what they learned, and share one more natural phrase live in the chat while they speak.

mistakes: If I studied harder, I would passed the exam.
If she takes the job, she would be happier.

title: Formal Reports: The Passive in Context
canDo: Can produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects, using a formal register and passive structures.
goal: Present findings and processes in a formal style using passive structures such as it is believed that.

warmup.prompt: Post this statement: Plastic bags should be banned in supermarkets. Ask: Do you agree? Give one reason in one sentence.
warmup.tutorAction: Give a short answer, then ask the student to restate their reason in a more formal way.

theory.structure: It is + past participle + that (formal reporting); subject + is / was / has been + past participle (passive for focus on the action)
examples: It is widely believed that recycling reduces waste.
The data has been analysed by three independent teams.
Several solutions were proposed during the meeting.
theory.method: Show a casual sentence beside its formal passive version. Ask guiding questions: Who does the action? Does the action matter more than the person? Let the student rewrite one casual sentence in the formal style.
theory.checkQuestion: In a formal report, do we usually name the person who did the action, or focus on the action?

comprehension.source: Read this report extract twice at native speed: It has been estimated that the new policy could save up to two million pounds a year. However, concerns were raised that the figures had not been independently verified.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What could the policy save? (up to two million pounds a year). What was not independently verified? (the figures).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the report sound confident or cautious? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the level of certainty, such as it has been estimated.

conversation.task: Briefing: the student presents a short, formal briefing on a topic of their choice (a policy, a product, a local issue) to the tutor, using at least three passive structures. The tutor asks two questions as a board member would.
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner. Challenge the student to use a formal register, and share a more precise word or phrase live in the chat as they speak.

mistakes: It is believe that recycling is good.
The data have analysed by three teams.

title: Contrast and Nuance: Advanced Linking Words
canDo: Can connect ideas with advanced linking words to build a clear, well-organised argument on abstract topics.
goal: Connect ideas using nevertheless, whereas, consequently, and in contrast to show nuance.

warmup.prompt: Post this question: Is it better to specialise in one subject or to study many? Ask: What is your view and why?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student answer instantly, then challenge them with one counter-argument.

theory.structure: Idea 1, whereas / while + idea 2 (contrast); Idea 1. Consequently, + result (cause and effect); Idea 1. Nevertheless, + idea 2 (concession)
examples: Some people prefer routine, whereas others enjoy variety.
Prices rose sharply. Consequently, many families cut back on spending.
The plan was risky. Nevertheless, the team decided to proceed.
theory.method: Show each linker with one example. Ask guiding questions: Does the second idea agree or contrast? Does it show a result or a concession? Let the student rewrite two simple sentences using one linker.
theory.checkQuestion: Does consequently introduce a result or a contrast?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at native speed: Urban planners often favour dense housing, whereas many residents prefer suburban gardens. Consequently, cities face a difficult trade-off between space and quality of life, and nevertheless, most planners remain optimistic.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What do urban planners favour? (dense housing). What do many residents prefer? (suburban gardens). What result does the text describe? (a difficult trade-off).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the writer balanced or does he or she favour one side? Ask the student to point to the word that shows the balance, such as whereas.

conversation.task: Trade-off debate: the student argues one side of a trade-off (remote learning versus classroom learning, city versus countryside) using at least three advanced linkers. The tutor counters with a point from the other side.
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner and language coach. Challenge the student to defend the trade-off, and share one stronger linker live in the chat while they speak.

mistakes: Some people like cities. Nevertheless they like countryside.
Prices rose, consequently families cut back.

title: Mixed Conditionals: Linking Past and Present
canDo: Can discuss how past events affect the present, and the consequences of unreal situations in detail.
goal: Explain how a past decision affects the present using mixed conditionals.

warmup.prompt: Post this question: If you had grown up in a different country, who would you be today?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student speculate for one minute, then ask one follow-up question to deepen the answer.

theory.structure: If + past perfect, would + base verb (past event, present result) or If + past simple, would have + past participle (present situation, past result)
examples: If I had taken the job, I would be living in London now.
If I were more confident, I would have applied last year.
If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor today.
theory.method: Show both mixed patterns with a timeline. Ask guiding questions: When did the cause happen? When is the result felt? Let the student create one mixed conditional about their own life.
theory.checkQuestion: In a mixed conditional, does the if-clause refer to the past and the main clause to the present, or the reverse?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at native speed: If the company had invested in training five years ago, it would not be struggling to find skilled staff today. Its managers now admit that if they were more proactive, the problem would be smaller.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What should the company have invested in five years ago? (training). What is the company struggling to find today? (skilled staff).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Do the managers sound defensive or accountable? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as admit.

conversation.task: Alternative lives: the student describes how their life would be different today if one past choice had gone another way. The tutor challenges them with one question: How would that affect your work or family now?
phrases: If I had ..., I would be ... now.
If I were ..., I would have ...
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner. Challenge the student to explain the present effect, and share one more natural phrase live in the chat while they speak.

mistakes: If I had studied law, I am a lawyer now.
If I was braver, I would applied last year.

title: Good Versus Better: Precise Word Choice
canDo: Can use a wide range of vocabulary to express precise meaning and avoid repetition in discussion.
goal: Replace basic verbs and adjectives with precise, professional alternatives in everyday discussion.

warmup.prompt: Post this sentence: The meeting was good and the team made a decision quickly. Ask: How would you describe this meeting more precisely?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student suggest one improvement, then ask for a second, more precise word.

theory.structure: Basic word (make, good, big) → precise word (reach a consensus, productive, substantial) in a matching collocation
examples: make a decision faster → speed up the decision process
a good result → a commendable outcome
a big problem → a considerable challenge
theory.method: Show three pairs on screen. Ask guiding questions: Is the new word more precise? Does it fit the same collocation? Let the student upgrade two sentences from their own week.
theory.checkQuestion: Which word is more precise in make a decision faster or speed up the decision process?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at native speed: The project went well, and the team reached a consensus quickly. The outcome was considerable, although the budget was a significant challenge at the start.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: How did the team reach agreement? (quickly, by consensus). What was a significant challenge? (the budget).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Does the writer describe the project as impressive or average? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as considerable.

conversation.task: Upgrade challenge: the student describes a recent project or event to the tutor, using at least five precise words instead of basic ones. The tutor responds naturally and asks one follow-up question.
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner. Type a more precise word into the live chat each time the student uses a basic one, without interrupting their sentence.

mistakes: The meeting was good and we made a decision fast.
It was a big problem for the team.

title: Idioms and Tone: Reading Between the Lines
canDo: Can understand implied meaning, idioms, and changes of tone in speech on familiar and abstract topics.
goal: Recognise idioms and tone in speech and use two or three of them naturally in discussion.

warmup.prompt: Post this sentence: Oh great, another meeting on Friday afternoon. Ask: How does the speaker feel? How do you know?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student identify the tone, then ask what words signal the tone.

theory.structure: Idiom or phrase (on the fence, bite the bullet, the ball is in your court) + literal meaning vs. intended meaning
examples: I am on the fence about the new offer. (I have not decided.)
We had to bite the bullet and cancel the trip. (We accepted an unpleasant choice.)
The ball is in your court now. (The next decision is yours.)
theory.method: Show each idiom with its literal and intended meaning. Ask guiding questions: Would the literal meaning make sense here? Let the student guess the meaning of a new idiom from context.
theory.checkQuestion: If someone says the ball is in your court, is the decision yours or theirs?

comprehension.source: Play a 45-second clip of a sarcastic conversation, or read this text twice at native speed: Sure, let's just add another deadline. It is not like the team is already stretched thin. Honestly, I am on the fence about whether we can deliver.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What is being added? (another deadline). Is the team already stretched? (yes, thin).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the first speaker serious or sarcastic? Ask the student to point to the words that show the tone, such as Sure and not like.

conversation.task: Office scenario roleplay: the tutor plays a manager who pushes an unreasonable deadline with sarcasm. The student replies diplomatically using at least two idioms and a tone that matches the situation.
phrases: I am on the fence about ...
We may have to bite the bullet ...
I think the ball is in ... court.
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner. Challenge the student to match the tone and avoid translating idioms from their native language. Share one better idiom live in the chat while they speak.

mistakes: I am in the fence about the offer.
We will bite the bullet and it is not good.

title: Negotiating Terms: Conditional Offers
canDo: Can negotiate and make conditional proposals in a real-time exchange, stating and weighing terms clearly.
goal: Make and respond to conditional offers in a negotiation using provided that and as long as.

warmup.prompt: Post this scenario: You are buying a used car, and the seller wants a higher price. Ask: What would you say first?
warmup.tutorAction: Let the student make an opening offer, then respond as the seller and ask one counter-question.

theory.structure: I am willing to + verb, provided that / as long as + condition; I could + verb, on condition that + condition
examples: I am willing to pay more, provided that the car has a full service record.
We can extend the deadline, as long as the quality remains the same.
I could lower the price on condition that you cover the transfer costs.
theory.method: Show the phrases with a short negotiation example. Ask guiding questions: What is offered? What is the condition? Let the student rephrase one of their own offers as a conditional offer.
theory.checkQuestion: In I can lower the price on condition that you pay the fee, which part is the condition?

comprehension.source: Read this text twice at native speed: The supplier is prepared to reduce the price, as long as the order is placed before the end of the month. However, the buyer would only accept the discount on condition that delivery is included.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What is the supplier prepared to reduce? (the price). When must the order be placed? (before the end of the month). What does the buyer require? (delivery included).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the buyer cooperative or firm? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the position, such as would only accept.

conversation.task: Real-time negotiation: the student negotiates a deal with the tutor (renting a flat, agreeing a project timeline, buying a product). Each offer must include a condition using provided that, as long as, or on condition that.
phrases: I am willing to ..., provided that ...
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner. Respond with realistic counter-offers and share one stronger phrase live in the chat when the student makes a weak offer.

mistakes: I will pay more if the car is good.
I can lower the price, on condition you pay.

title: Persuasive Speaking: Making a Case to an Audience
canDo: Can deliver clear, detailed presentations and sustain a persuasive case on a topical issue in front of listeners.
goal: Deliver a two-minute persuasive case using a clear structure, precise vocabulary, and a strong close.

warmup.prompt: Post this topic: Should schools teach financial skills? Ask: Take thirty seconds to give your position.
warmup.tutorAction: Ask the student to state a position immediately, then challenge it with one counter-point.

theory.structure: Hook + thesis + two supporting points + concession + call to action
examples: Imagine leaving school without knowing how to open a bank account. (hook)
My view is that financial education should be compulsory. (thesis)
Ultimately, the choice is clear, so let us act now. (call to action)
theory.method: Show the five-part frame on screen. Ask guiding questions: Which part grabs attention? Where is the concession? Let the student map their warm-up position onto the frame.
theory.checkQuestion: Which part of the speech asks the audience to act?

comprehension.source: Read this speech extract twice at native speed: Imagine a world where every young person can manage their own money. Critics say schools are already overloaded, yet financial skills affect every decision we make, so they belong in the classroom.
comprehension.factCheck: Ask: What does the speaker imagine? (a world where young people manage their own money). What do critics say? (schools are overloaded).
comprehension.toneCheck: Ask: Is the speaker confident or hesitant? Ask the student to point to the phrase that shows the attitude, such as so they belong.

conversation.task: Two-minute persuasive speech: the student delivers a short speech to the tutor, who acts as a sceptical audience member and asks one challenging question at the end. The student must use the five-part frame.
conversation.mandate: Act as a conversation partner and sceptical listener. Challenge the student to defend the speech, and share one stronger phrase live in the chat while they speak.

mistakes: Imagine a school, the kids dont know money.
My opinion is that money education is important very much.
